strengths: Addresses an important problem: retaining information beyond the context window of offline reinforcement-learning policies without attending to the entire trajectory.

The T-Maze results provide concrete evidence of long-horizon retention: RATE achieves approximately 90% success at length 900 after training on lengths up to 90. Table 6 also shows that MRV improves success from 61% to 90% at length 900 under the ablation configuration.
The evaluation covers four memory-intensive environments, four Atari games, and nine MuJoCo settings, with substantial improvements over DT on ViZDoom and several standard benchmarks.

Pillar-removal controls, memory-corruption experiments, alternative MRV configurations, and hyperparameter studies provide useful diagnostic evidence. Dataset descriptions, repeated runs, hyperparameters, and a code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. RATE combines established RMT memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching, while MRV is standard cross-attention between successive memory states. The paper needs a sharper account of its advance over existing recurrent and gated transformer memory architectures.

Important comparisons do not isolate the proposed memory mechanisms. Appendix D disables feed-forward blocks only for RATE and introduces segment-wise target-return resets for its MuJoCo evaluation. Without matched ablations, performance gains and memory savings cannot be cleanly attributed to recurrent memory or MRV.

Evidence for broad superiority is mixed. Memory Maze improves only from RMT's 7.27 ± 0.21 to 7.64 ± 0.41, with three training runs and no convincing uncertainty analysis of the difference. On Minigrid, other memory baselines outperform RATE in different length regimes. Its MuJoCo mean also trails the two Mamba baselines. The strongest retention evidence concerns a single binary cue; richer memory capacity remains untested.

The recurrent-baseline results require stronger validation. LSTM, GRU, and Mamba all achieve exactly chance performance on T-Maze even at the training horizon of 90. Without documented architecture-specific tuning or failure diagnostics, these results do not establish the claimed inability of these model families to handle sparse long-term dependencies.

Several implementation and resource-reporting details are incomplete or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 omits cache updates and inter-segment gradient handling; Algorithm 2 omits the MRV activation specified in Table 8. Appendix G's parameter-overhead formula counts only memory embeddings, ignoring MRV projection matrices and the feed-forward-block removal, undermining the claimed parameter comparison.

The asserted OracleDT upper bound is unjustified. Providing privileged information to a separately trained model does not guarantee the ordering R[OracleDT] ≥ R[RATE] ≥ R[DT], since optimization and model classes differ. Table 5 supplies an informative reference performance, not a guaranteed bound.
